Replace elections with sortition. At first glance, that sentence seems to upend two centuries of American habit. But look beyond habit to incentives, and a stark truth appears: elections as we run them today manufacture corruption, entrench partisanship, and sideline ordinary people. A civic lottery that drafts representative samples of citizens to legislate and to serve fixed, short terms in executive leadership would transform those incentives. It would remove the money-chasing machinery that distorts public life, short-circuit the partisan arms race, and empower the very people our Constitution purports to serve. Far from a utopian fantasy, sortition is a practical, proven tool—one Americans already trust every day when we empanel juries to decide matters of life and liberty.

How sortition would work

  • A civic lottery randomly selects citizens from the whole adult population, stratified to mirror the community’s demographics. Eligibility screens exclude serious conflicts of interest and recent high-level lobbyists, and provide accommodations for caregiving, disability, or hardship.
  • Selected citizens serve for short, staggered terms—say one to two years in a legislature; six to twelve months on an executive council—receiving a living stipend, job protection, and training.
  • Deliberation is supported by a professional, nonpartisan civil service. Mini-publics hear from competing experts, stakeholders, and advocates, then debate in small groups before making decisions by majority or supermajority.
  • Transparency is mandatory: sessions are recorded, votes are public, lobbying contacts are logged, and the selection algorithm is open-source and auditable.
  • Strict ethics rules, anti-bribery enforcement, and cooling-off periods prevent personal enrichment and revolving-door influence.

These are not abstractions. Athens used sortition to staff most public offices for 150 years. The Venetian Republic selected its Doge through layered lotteries to foil factional capture. In our own time, citizens’ assemblies in Ireland helped shepherd major constitutional changes with surprising consensus, British Columbia and Oregon used sortition to deliberate on electoral reforms, and Belgium’s German-speaking community has a permanent citizens’ council steering its agenda. Time and again, ordinary people—given time, information, and a fair process—produce judgments that are balanced, humane, and resistant to capture.

Why sortition dismantles corruption at the root Corruption flourishes where politicians must raise money and cling to office. Elections create a permanent market for influence: donors bundle, lobbyists dangle future jobs, and officeholders trade access for advantage. Even well-meaning candidates are forced into this economy; the price of admission is dependence.

Sortition removes the market. If officials are chosen by lot:

  • There is nothing to buy. You cannot bankroll a winning campaign when there is no campaign.
  • Bribery is riskier and less effective. No one knows who will be selected in the next round, terms are short and non-renewable, and decision-making is distributed across many citizens—raising the cost and lowering the payoff of corrupt overtures.
  • Revolving-door temptations shrink. With a strict post-service cooling-off period and no career to build, the typical leverage points for interest groups vanish.
  • Time and attention are reclaimed. Instead of spending hours fundraising and messaging, citizen-officials spend their limited service deliberating.

We have an American analogue: juries. Because jurors are randomly selected, paid, temporarily sequestered from pressure, and subject to penalties for misconduct, the justice system treats their decisions as legitimate and largely free from financial contamination. We can design civic juries and councils to meet the same high bar.

Why sortition defuses partisanship Elections reward polarization. In an era of gerrymandered districts and closed primaries, candidates win by energizing bases, not by persuading opposites. Outrage, not nuance, is the fuel of victory. Once elected, officials are bound to party machines that control committee assignments, fundraising, and future prospects.

A lottery breaks the logic loop:

  • No primaries, no gerrymanders, no base to stoke. Random selection yields bodies that reflect the electorate in all its variety, not just the most motivated fraction.
  • No reelection anxiety. Without a next race to win, the incentive becomes solving the problem at hand, not scoring points.
  • Deliberation replaces debate-clubbing. When people are not performing for cameras or donors, and when the process brings experts from multiple sides, participants tend to update their views and seek workable compromises.
  • Parties shrink to ideas. Without candidate slates to control, political parties can still supply platforms and policy proposals—but not dominate the staffing of government.

The result is not a mushy centrism. It is a practical public-spiritedness born of proximity to diverse neighbors and the absence of partisan reward structures. Studies of deliberative mini-publics consistently find that random citizens, given time and fair information, move away from extremes toward informed, often creative consensus.

Why sortition empowers ordinary people Elections concentrate power in a political class: those who can raise money, endure the campaign gauntlet, and speak in media-approved ways. Whole talents—quiet competence, deep local knowledge, vocational expertise, caregiving wisdom—rarely surface in that tournament.

A civic lottery treats citizenship as a qualification in itself:

  • Equal chance, equal dignity. Every eligible adult has a genuine chance to legislate and govern. Representation becomes descriptive by design, not by hope.
  • Barriers fall. Money, insider networks, and media prowess stop being gateways.
  • Civic skills scale. Training, facilitation, and service experience transform participants—and, through them, their communities. People return home as resources, not spectators.
  • Trust rebounds. Seeing neighbors in the room, not career politicians, rebuilds legitimacy. Government becomes “us” again.

What about competence, accountability, and stability? These are the most common concerns. They are real—and addressable in design.

Competence. We already trust random citizens with serious judgment in juries. The remedy is process: provide balanced briefings; require agencies to supply options and impact analyses; invite adversarial experts; use skilled facilitators; and structure decisions with clear timelines and supermajority thresholds for irreversible actions. Professional civil servants remain in place to execute policy and ensure continuity.

Accountability. Elections are a blunt accountability tool; they punish or reward slogans, not specific decisions, and they are easily gamed by money and media. Sortition substitutes direct, rule-bound accountability:

  • Codes of conduct, conflict-of-interest rules, and financial disclosures.
  • Public transparency of meetings, vote records, and contacts with lobbyists.
  • Independent inspectors general and ethics commissions empowered to investigate, sanction, and remove for cause.
  • Judicial review to protect constitutional rights and check overreach.
  • Citizen oversight panels—also selected by lot—auditing performance.

Stability. Rotation can be designed to preserve institutional memory: staggered terms, overlapping cohorts, and professional staff sustain continuity. For the executive, a multi-member council chosen by lot, with portfolios assigned and a professional cabinet, prevents whiplash while avoiding the concentration of power in a single election-dependent figure.

A credible path to get there Wholesale constitutional change will take time and persuasion. That is an argument for piloting, not for paralysis.

  • Start local. Replace appointed boards and low-turnout municipal elections with civic lotteries. Many jurisdictions already use sortition for planning commissions, policing oversight, and budgeting councils.
  • Institutionalize citizens’ assemblies. Use them to set legislative agendas, review major bills, and propose charters or constitutional amendments. Their track record worldwide shows they can tackle thorny questions responsibly.
  • Hybridize and expand. States can adopt one legislative chamber by lot while retaining the other by election; use random selection for powerful ethics boards, redistricting commissions, and appropriations oversight. As trust grows, expand.
  • Amend constitutionally, not by stealth. Ultimately, replacing elections at state and federal levels will require formal amendments. A network of successful pilots provides the evidence and confidence to do so.

The American fit Sortition is not an import alien to American values. It is a restoration of first principles.

  • Anti-faction: The Founders feared factions; elections have supercharged them. A lottery diffuses factional power by making capture unpredictable and temporary.
  • Civic equality: One person, one vote is noble—but in practice, wealth and mobilization distort it. One person, equal chance to serve delivers what equality promises.
  • Republican virtue: The ideal of the citizen-legislator—someone who serves briefly, then returns home—was central to the early republic. Sortition makes it the rule, not the exception.
  • Jury tradition: We already enshrine the idea that ordinary people, selected by lot, can weigh evidence and do justice. Extending that trust from verdicts to policies is a natural next step.

The cost of clinging to elections as we practice them is visible all around us: paralyzed legislatures, performative hearings, policy whiplash, information warfare, gerrymandered maps, pay-to-play access, and corrosive cynicism. We have optimized a system for winning, not for governing. Sortition flips the optimization toward deliberation, common sense, and the public interest.

Replacing elections with sortition is not a rejection of democracy; it is democracy refined. It removes the structural incentives for corruption, drains the fuel from hyperpartisanship, and invites every American—not just the wealthy, the loud, or the connected—into the work of self-government. If we want a politics worthy of our people, we should trust our people to do the politics.

The Lottery of Liberty: Why Sortition Must Replace Elections in America

We live in an age of profound democratic disillusionment. Voter turnout languishes, approval ratings for Congress dip into the teens, and the corrosive influence of money in politics is an accepted, if lamented, fact of life. The foundational ritual of our republic—the election—has become a theater of the absurd, a billion-dollar spectacle that produces leaders more beholden to donors and party bases than to the common good. It is time to discard this failed mechanism and embrace a system that truly reflects the foundational principle of democracy: that power derives from the people, not from the manipulation of their passions. That system is sortition—the random selection of citizens to serve in legislative and executive office. Replacing elections with sortition is not a utopian fantasy; it is a pragmatic, revolutionary step necessary to excise political corruption, dismantle toxic partisanship, and finally empower ordinary people as the true governors of their nation.

The most urgent argument for sortition is its unparalleled ability to eradicate political corruption. The current electoral system is a pay-to-play scheme disguised as a contest of ideas. Candidates, to be viable, must devote the majority of their time not to studying policy or meeting constituents, but to dialing for dollars from a tiny pool of wealthy individuals, corporate PACs, and special interest groups. The result is a legalized system of bribery: votes are traded for campaign checks, and legislation is crafted to reward benefactors. Lobbyists don't just influence lawmaking; they own it. Sortition dismantles this entire corrupt infrastructure at its root. A randomly selected citizen, serving a single, nonrenewable term, would have no campaign to fund. There would be no donor class to appease, no future election to rig. Their sole allegiance would be to their conscience, their newfound duty, and the informed judgment they develop while in office. The revolving door between Congress and K Street would slam shut, for there would be no "former officeholder" to lobby. Power would no longer be a commodity to be bought, but a temporary public trust, arbitrarily but justly bestowed.

Closely related is sortition’s power to neutralize the scourge of hyper-partisanship that paralyzes American governance. Our electoral system is explicitly designed to create division. Primary elections reward extremism, as candidates cater to the most activist, ideologically rigid segments of their base. General elections become tribal bloodbaths, with parties investing billions to paint the opposition as an existential threat. Governing becomes not about pragmatic problem-solving, but about perpetual campaigning and base mobilization. Sortition obliterates this dynamic. A truly random sample of the citizenry is a microcosm of the nation—politically, racially, socioeconomically, and ideologically diverse. It would include fervent Democrats, staunch Republicans, passionate independents, and the politically disengaged. Forced to deliberate and decide together, these ordinary Americans would have no choice but to seek common ground. Their shared identity as citizens, not as party members, would become the operative framework. Compromise would not be a sign of weakness but a necessity for a group representing the full spectrum of their community. The toxic zero-sum game of electoral politics would give way to the practical art of collaborative governance.

Finally, and most profoundly, sortition is the only system that can genuinely empower ordinary people. Elections create a political class—a separate caste of professional politicians, operatives, and pundits who speak a specialized language and live in a world divorced from the daily realities of most Americans. Sortition tears down that wall. It declares that the wisdom, experience, and common sense of a teacher, a nurse, a mechanic, or a small-business owner are not just as valuable as those of a career politician, but more valuable, precisely because they are uncorrupted by the system. It is a system of participatory rather than representative democracy. When your neighbor, your coworker, or the person you see at the grocery store is randomly chosen to serve, democracy becomes tangible. It fosters a sense of civic ownership and responsibility that voting once every two years cannot match. It educates the populace not through soundbites, but through direct, hands-on experience in governance. The knowledge that anyone could be called to serve strengthens the social contract and reinforces the idea that the state belongs to the people, not to the parties.

Critics will raise familiar objections. The most common is the "expertise" argument: governance requires specialized knowledge that randomly selected citizens lack. This is a red herring. Our current system selects not for expertise, but for charisma, fundraising ability, and ideological purity. Sortition bodies would, by necessity, rely on and empower professional, nonpartisan staff—scientists, economists, military analysts—whose advice would be sought to inform decisions, not to dictate them. The deliberative body itself would bring the essential, often missing, expertise of lived experience. Another objection is stability: would a rotating cast of amateurs produce coherent, long-term policy? The answer lies in the design: a sortition legislature could be structured with staggered, multi-year terms, and a separate, randomly selected executive council could provide continuity. The goal is not chaos, but a government periodically infused with fresh, unjaded perspectives.

The philosophical foundation for sortition is ancient and noble. The Athenians, the inventors of democracy, used it for the vast majority of their public offices. The Venetian Republic, for all its faults, used a complex system of sortition to select its leader, the Doge, precisely to prevent the consolidation of factional power. In our own time, we have seen the power of sortition in action. Ireland’s Citizens' Assembly, a randomly selected body that deliberated on issues like abortion and climate change, broke decades of political deadlock and produced recommendations that led to constitutional change. Its legitimacy stemmed from its demographic mirror of the nation and its freedom from electoral fear.

The United States was founded on a radical idea: that the people are capable of self-government. We have allowed that idea to atrophy, replacing it with a managed, money-driven, and divisive spectacle. Sortition is not a rejection of democracy, but its ultimate fulfillment. It is the mechanism by which we can finally have a government that is of the people, by the people, and for the people—not the people as an abstract mass to be manipulated every four years, but the living, breathing, diverse citizenry, called upon to serve their nation with the solemn duty and fresh eyes that only random selection can provide. To save our republic, we must cast the lot, not the ballot. The future of American democracy depends on it.

Excellent question. Sortition, or the random selection of citizens for political office, is a concept with deep historical roots (most famously in Athenian democracy) and a growing modern revival, particularly for upper houses or advisory bodies. Advocates argue it can fundamentally reshape governance along the lines you've outlined.

Here’s a breakdown of the supposed benefits and reasons for a nationwide sortition system, focusing on fairness, reducing elite influence, and enhancing representation.

1. Improving Government Fairness

  • Leveling the Playing Field: Traditional elections are massively influenced by wealth, name recognition, and access to media. Sortition eliminates the "candidate selection" phase entirely. Anyone who meets basic eligibility criteria (age, citizenship, no felony record) has an equal, random chance of service. This removes the inherent unfairness of a system where only the wealthy, well-connected, or charismatic can realistically compete.
  • Eliminating Campaign Distortion: Campaigns incentivize simplistic messaging, pandering, and negative attacks. Sortition removes the need for campaigning, allowing selected individuals to focus solely on policy deliberation and learning, rather than fundraising and optics.
  • Randomness as a Fairness Mechanism: Just as a jury is meant to be a cross-section of the community, a randomly selected legislature is designed to be a microcosm of the citizenry. This is seen as inherently fairer than a body chosen by a sometimes-small, unrepresentative fraction of the electorate (primary voters, party activists).

2. Reducing Elite Influence

  • Breaking the Career Politician Class: Sortition would prevent the formation of a permanent political class with its own interests, incentives, and culture often disconnected from the general public. Legislators would be ordinary citizens temporarily called to service, like jury duty.
  • Curbing Corporate & Special Interest Power: Lobbying and campaign donations are the primary tools for influencing elected officials. In a sortition system, there are no re-election campaigns to fund. While advocates acknowledge that selected citizens could still be lobbied, the lack of a permanent, re-electable target and the temporary nature of the role would drastically reduce the return on investment for special interest spending.
  • Disrupting the "Revolving Door": With no future in politics, there is no incentive for a selected official to cultivate relationships with industries for a future lobbying job. This severs a key channel of post-service corruption.

3. Enhancing Democratic Representation

  • Descriptive Representation: A randomly selected body, if the pool is the entire citizenry, will statistically mirror the population in terms of gender, race, class, occupation, and life experience. This is its most powerful argument. A 2023 poll of the U.S. Congress, for example, would show it is disproportionately white, male, wealthy, and college-educated compared to the nation. Sortition would correct this imbalance not by policy, but by pure probability.
  • Elevging Experiential Knowledge: A legislature of randomly selected teachers, nurses, engineers, small business owners, and retirees would bring a vast reservoir of practical, lived experience to policy debates—experience that is often missing from legislatures dominated by lawyers and career politicians.
  • Reducing Polarization: Without the need to constantly appeal to a party base or fear primary challengers, selected citizens might be more willing to engage in good-faith negotiation and compromise. The goal shifts from "winning" for one's party to "solving" for one's community.
  • Restoring Trust: When citizens see their own neighbors—not a remote, professional political class—making decisions, it can increase the perceived legitimacy of government and reduce feelings of alienation and distrust.

How It Might Function (A Common Model)

A typical proposal for a sortition-based legislative chamber might work like this:

  1. A large, random pool of eligible citizens is selected from the census.
  2. From this pool, a smaller group (e.g., 300-500) is randomly chosen to serve a fixed, non-renewable term (e.g., 3 years).
  3. This "Citizen's Assembly" would have primary law-making authority, perhaps with a suspensive veto for a smaller, elected "Review Chamber" or the executive.
  4. Members would receive a living stipend and professional staff support to allow them to serve effectively.

Important Caveats and Counterarguments

Proponents are not blind to challenges:

  • Competence: Critics argue that random selection does not guarantee expertise, wisdom, or the ability to resist demagoguery or sophisticated lobbying. Advocates respond that a well-supported, diverse body with access to expert testimony can be highly competent and that elected bodies are not guaranteed competence either.
  • Legitimacy: Would people accept laws made by "common folks" over "experienced leaders"? Advocates say legitimacy would come from the body's perfect descriptiveness and the fairness of the random process.
  • The "Sorting" Problem: Who designs the lottery? Could it be gamed? This requires robust, transparent, and apolitical administration (perhaps by a judiciary body).
  • Not a Panacea: Most serious proposals see sortition as a complement to, not a complete replacement for, elections—perhaps for an upper house or specific constitutional reform assemblies. A pure sortition system for all branches (especially a head of state or foreign policy) is rarer.

Conclusion

To understand the urgency of adopting sortition, we must first confront the glaring failures of the current electoral system. Elections in the United States are heavily influenced by money, with candidates relying on massive campaign contributions often provided by corporations, lobbyists, and wealthy donors. This dynamic breeds corruption, as politicians prioritize the interests of the elite over the needs of the average citizen—whether it’s passing tax cuts for the wealthy or deregulating industries at the expense of environmental or public health protections.

Moreover, elections exacerbate partisanship, dividing the nation into increasingly hostile camps. This has led to a political landscape marked by gridlock, where compromise is seen as weakness and governance suffers as a result. Those who do run are often career politicians or individuals with connections to political machines, perpetuating a ruling class disconnected from the lived experiences of most Americans. Voter turnout remains dismally low—often hovering around 60% in presidential elections and far lower in midterms and local races—reflecting widespread disillusionment with a system that seems unresponsive to the needs of the people.

Sortition, the random selection of citizens to serve in governmental roles, offers a radical yet profoundly democratic alternative to elections. This concept is not new; it was a cornerstone of ancient Athenian democracy, where citizens were chosen by lot to serve in legislative and judicial roles. In a modern context, sortition would involve randomly selecting a representative sample of citizens to serve in Congress, state legislatures, and even executive positions like governor or president, with appropriate checks to ensure competence and accountability (such as advisory boards or recall mechanisms). By randomly selecting leaders from the general population, we eliminate the influence of money, political parties, and personal ambition from the process of governance. Instead of a system where power is concentrated in the hands of a self-perpetuating elite, sortition ensures that governance reflects the diversity of the American populace—across race, class, gender, and geography. In the current system, elected officials often face immense pressure to court donors and special interest groups to fund their campaigns. Sortition removes this dynamic entirely. Because leaders are chosen randomly rather than through campaigns, there are no elections to finance, no donors to appease, and no quid pro quo arrangements to be made. A citizen selected by lot would have no prior allegiance to lobbyists or corporate interests, nor would they have a personal incentive to prioritize reelection over the public good. Their only mandate would be to serve the interests of their fellow citizens during their limited term.

Moreover, sortition reduces the risk of entrenched power. Elected officials often become career politicians, building networks of influence and loyalty that insulate them from accountability. In contrast, sortition ensures a constant rotation of fresh perspectives, with citizens serving for a defined period before returning to private life. This prevents the formation of a permanent political class and minimizes opportunities for corruption to take root. While no system is immune to individual misconduct, sortition’s structural design—rooted in randomness and temporariness—creates far fewer incentives for unethical behavior than the current electoral model.

Sortition offers a bold and necessary alternative—a system that dismantles the influence of money and power, reduces the scourge of partisanship, and empowers ordinary citizens to take control of their government. Introduction

Despite claims of democracy, millions of Americans feel unheard. Minority groups, the working class, and rural communities are often ignored in favor of wealthy urban elites. Elections favor those with name recognition, media access, and financial backing, leaving ordinary people without a voice.

1. True Democracy in Action

Sortition is the purest form of democracy. In ancient Athens, the birthplace of democracy, key government positions were filled by lottery to prevent corruption and ensure fairness. 2. Reduced Political Corruption

When leaders are chosen randomly, they cannot be bought or manipulated. There would be no need for campaign financing, no lobbyist influence, and no backroom deals. Public office would become a civic duty rather than a career path for the ambitious and connected.

Change is necessary when the current system is broken. The Founding Fathers themselves were skeptical of pure democracy, fearing mob rule. Sortition offers a middle ground—a system that is both democratic and resistant to manipulation.

Conclusion

The United States claims to be a democracy, yet its electoral system is undemocratic in practice. Sortition offers a revolutionary but practical solution: a government truly of, by, and for the people. By removing corruption, reducing partisanship, and empowering ordinary citizens, sortition would restore faith in democracy and ensure that political power is not concentrated in the hands of the few.

Introduction

We create a system where the government truly is a microcosm of the people, where leadership is a public service, not a path to private power. Modern electoral democracies often suffer from a "democratic deficit" where the government does not look like the people it governs.   • Professional vs. Citizen Governance: Elections often favor those with professional political experience (career politicians). 3. Improving Government Fairness and Depolarization

Elections are inherently competitive and adversarial. To win, politicians often must frame issues as a binary conflict ("us vs. them"), fueling polarization and partisan warfare.

  • Incentivizing Compromise: Because sortition members serve limited terms and do not need to campaign for re-election, they are freed from the pressure of pleasing a partisan base. This allows them to vote based on evidence and the long-term public good rather than short-term electoral survival.

Applying sortition to the executive branch (e.g., a President or Prime Minister) is more radical than applying it to a legislature, but proponents offer specific theoretical frameworks:

One of the deepest criticisms of modern democracy is voter apathy. Many citizens feel their vote has no impact, leading to disengagement and cynicism.

The core argument for sortition is that it changes the incentive structure of governance. In an electoral system, the politician asks: "What do I need to do to get re-elected?" In a sortition system, the official asks: "How do I use my time to fulfill the mandate of my peers?"

Model Response:

The Lottery of Liberty: A Case for Replacing Elections with Sortition in the United States

Introduction

The United States was born from a revolutionary premise: that ordinary people possess the wisdom, dignity, and right to govern themselves. Yet the mechanism chosen to realize that premise—competitive elections—has, over nearly 250 years, metastasized into something the founders would scarcely recognize and would likely abhor. Elections were meant to be a tool of self-governance. They have become instead a tool of self-enrichment for a permanent political class, a theater of tribal warfare between ideological factions, and an elaborate ritual that provides the illusion of popular sovereignty while concentrating real power in the hands of wealthy donors, party elites, and career politicians. The American experiment in democracy is faltering not because democracy was the wrong ideal, but because elections are the wrong instrument.

There is, however, an older instrument—one tested in the cradle of democracy itself—that deserves serious reconsideration. Sortition, the selection of political officeholders by random lot from the citizen population, offers a radical but historically grounded alternative to electoral politics. Under a comprehensive sortition system, the members of Congress, state legislatures, city councils, and even key executive officeholders would not be elected through campaigns and voting but would instead be randomly selected from the eligible citizenry, much as jurors are selected today. They would serve defined terms, receive training, access expert testimony, and deliberate on the public's behalf before returning to private life.

This essay argues that the United States should replace its current electoral system with a robust and carefully designed system of sortition. Such a transformation would dismantle the structural corruption that poisons American governance, neutralize the hyper-partisanship that paralyzes it, and restore genuine power to the ordinary citizens in whose name government purportedly operates. The case for sortition is not utopian fantasy. It is a practical, evidence-supported, and philosophically compelling answer to the most dangerous pathologies of modern American political life.

I. The Crisis of Electoral Democracy

Before arguing for the alternative, it is essential to understand the depth of the disease. American elections are not functioning as instruments of democratic accountability. They are functioning as instruments of oligarchic reproduction.

Consider the numbers. In the 2020 election cycle, total spending on federal campaigns exceeded $14 billion, more than doubling the figure from just four years earlier. Members of Congress spend between 30 and 70 percent of their time in office fundraising, according to reports from departing legislators of both parties. The winner of a U.S. Senate race now spends, on average, over $10 million. This is not a system that selects for wisdom, empathy, or public-spiritedness. It is a system that selects for the ability to raise money and the willingness to be indebted to those who provide it.

Consider the sociology. The 117th Congress was composed overwhelmingly of lawyers, businesspeople, and career politicians. The median net worth of a member of Congress vastly exceeds that of a typical American household. Women, racial minorities, working-class people, and those without college degrees remain dramatically underrepresented relative to their share of the population. Elections, for all their democratic romance, consistently elevate a narrow social stratum—those with connections, resources, name recognition, and the peculiar appetite for self-promotion that campaigning requires.

Consider the outcomes. Major peer-reviewed studies, most notably the 2014 analysis by Martin Gilens and Benjamin Page at Princeton and Northwestern, have demonstrated that the policy preferences of average Americans have near-zero statistical impact on the probability that a given policy will be adopted, while the preferences of economic elites and organized interest groups have substantial and significant influence. The conclusion is stark: the United States already functions less as a democracy and more as an oligarchy with democratic trappings. Elections are the trappings.

Consider the psychology. Partisan polarization has reached levels not seen since the years preceding the Civil War. Scholars such as Lilliana Mason have documented that political identity in America has become a "mega-identity," fusing partisan affiliation with racial, religious, geographic, and cultural identity into tribal allegiances that make compromise feel like betrayal. Elections do not cause this polarization by themselves, but they provide the gladiatorial arena in which it escalates. Campaigns are incentivized to demonize opponents, mobilize fear, and reduce complex policy questions to binary tribal signals. Every two years, the country submits itself to a ritual of collective rage that leaves governance more difficult afterward.

The standard reform proposals—campaign finance regulation, ranked-choice voting, independent redistricting commissions, term limits—are worthy incremental measures, but they are bandages on a hemorrhage. They attempt to make elections work better while ignoring the possibility that elections themselves are the structural source of the dysfunction. Sortition addresses the problem at its root.

II. The Principle of Sortition: Ancient Wisdom, Modern Application

Sortition is not a novel invention conjured from abstract theory. It is the original democratic method, practiced for nearly two centuries in Athens, the civilization that gave democracy its name and its founding ideals.

In Athenian democracy during the fifth and fourth centuries BCE, the vast majority of public offices were filled by lot. The Boule, a council of 500 citizens that set the legislative agenda and oversaw administration, was composed entirely of randomly selected citizens who served one-year terms. Magistracies, jury panels, and oversight boards were similarly staffed through lottery. The Athenians considered elections to be an aristocratic device—a method that inevitably favored the wealthy, the well-known, and the rhetorically gifted—and they reserved elections only for a handful of positions requiring specialized military or financial expertise. Aristotle himself articulated this distinction clearly: "The appointment of magistrates by lot is thought to be democratic, and the election of them oligarchical."

The Athenian insight was not naive. They understood that random selection, combined with institutional design—short terms, rotation requirements, accountability mechanisms, collective deliberation—could produce governance that was both competent and genuinely representative of the citizen body as a whole. Modern political theorists have revived and refined this insight. Alexander Guerrero's concept of "lottocracy," Hélène Landemore's work on "democratic reason" and the epistemic virtues of cognitive diversity, and the practical experiments conducted through citizens' assemblies around the world have given sortition a rigorous contemporary intellectual foundation.

The modern case for sortition does not require replicating Athens exactly. It requires applying the core principle—random selection from the eligible population—within institutional structures designed for modern complexity. A contemporary sortition system for the United States might look something like this:

  • Legislative bodies (the House of Representatives, state legislatures, city councils) would be composed of citizens selected by stratified random sampling from the eligible adult population, ensuring demographic representativeness across dimensions of geography, race, gender, age, income, and education.
  • Selected citizens would serve fixed terms (perhaps two to three years), during which they would receive a generous salary, job protection guarantees, and comprehensive orientation.
  • Deliberative infrastructure would be built into the legislative process: selected citizens would have access to nonpartisan research staff, expert witnesses representing diverse perspectives, structured deliberation protocols, and facilitated small-group discussions before voting on legislation.
  • Executive functions could be handled by councils or commissions selected by lot, or by professional administrators appointed by and accountable to the sortition-based legislature, rather than by a single elected executive.
  • Accountability mechanisms would include post-service review, transparency requirements, and the regular rotation of new randomly selected citizens into office.

This is not chaos. It is structured, deliberative, and representative government—more genuinely representative, in fact, than anything elections have ever produced.

III. Sortition Eliminates Political Corruption

The most powerful argument for sortition is its capacity to destroy the structural incentives that produce political corruption. Corruption in American politics is not primarily a matter of individual moral failure. It is a predictable consequence of institutional design. Elections create a dependency relationship between officeholders and funders that no amount of regulation has been able to sever.

Sortition eliminates the campaign finance problem entirely. If there are no campaigns, there is no campaign spending. If there is no campaign spending, there is no need for fundraising. If there is no fundraising, there is no dependency on donors. The entire architecture of legalized corruption—super PACs, bundlers, dark money organizations, the revolving door between lobbying firms and congressional offices—collapses when the pathway to power is a random lottery rather than a fundraising competition. No corporation writes a check to a random number generator. No billionaire hosts a fundraising dinner for the laws of probability.

This is not a marginal improvement. It is the complete elimination of the single most corrosive force in American governance. For decades, reformers have tried to regulate the flow of money into politics through legislation (the Federal Election Campaign Act, the Bipartisan Campaign Reform Act) and have watched the Supreme Court systematically dismantle those regulations in the name of free speech (Buckley v. Valeo, Citizens United v. FEC, McCutcheon v. FEC). The Court has held, in essence, that spending money on campaigns is constitutionally protected expression. Sortition renders this entire legal and political struggle moot. You cannot constitutionally protect the right to spend money influencing an election if there is no election to influence.

Sortition also eliminates the career incentive that distorts officeholders' behavior. A fundamental problem with elected legislators is that their primary professional objective is reelection. This means that every vote, every public statement, every committee action is filtered through the question: "How will this affect my next campaign?" The result is systematic cowardice. Legislators avoid difficult but necessary decisions (reforming entitlement programs, addressing long-term climate policy, closing popular but inefficient military bases) because the short-term political costs outweigh the long-term public benefits. Randomly selected citizens who serve a single term and then return to private life have no reelection incentive. They can afford to think about the long-term public good because they have no political future to protect.

Lobbying itself is transformed under sortition. The current lobbying industry is effective because it operates on a small, stable, and predictable set of targets: 535 members of Congress who serve for years or decades and develop ongoing relationships with industry representatives. Under sortition, the legislative body is constantly rotating, unpredictable, and too large and diverse to be efficiently captured. Lobbyists cannot build long-term dependency relationships with legislators who serve briefly and are replaced by a new random cohort. The economics of lobbying fundamentally change when your targets are temporary, numerous, and unknown in advance.

IV. Sortition Neutralizes Hyper-Partisanship

America's two-party system has produced a level of partisan hostility that threatens the basic capacity for governance. Sortition does not merely reduce partisanship; it removes the structural conditions that generate it.

Political parties exist because elections exist. Parties are organizations designed to contest elections—to recruit candidates, mobilize voters, raise money, and coordinate campaign strategy. Without elections, parties lose their primary reason for being. Under sortition, there are no candidates to recruit, no voters to mobilize, no campaigns to wage. Parties might continue to exist as ideological associations or advocacy organizations, but they would wield nothing like the power they currently hold. The party leadership could not threaten a randomly selected legislator with a primary challenge, withhold committee assignments based on party loyalty, or discipline members who break ranks on key votes. The entire apparatus of partisan coercion dissolves.

The tribal psychology of partisanship is fed by the adversarial structure of campaigns. Elections are, by design, competitive. They pit candidates against each other and, by extension, pit their supporters against each other. Media coverage amplifies conflict because conflict drives engagement. Political consultants design messaging to activate fear and anger because those emotions drive voter turnout. The result is a permanent cycle of escalating hostility in which fellow citizens come to view each other not as neighbors with different perspectives but as existential threats. Sortition replaces this adversarial structure with a deliberative one. Randomly selected citizens, drawn from across the political spectrum, sit together in a room and work through problems collaboratively. The evidence from citizens' assemblies consistently shows that this process reduces polarization, builds mutual understanding, and produces consensus on issues that elected legislatures find intractable.

The evidence from real-world deliberative bodies is striking. Ireland's Citizens' Assembly, composed of 99 randomly selected citizens, deliberated on the question of abortion rights—one of the most polarizing issues in Irish politics—and produced a recommendation that led to a successful constitutional referendum in 2018. The British Columbia Citizens' Assembly on Electoral Reform, the French Citizens' Convention on Climate, the German citizens' councils on various policy questions—all have demonstrated that randomly selected citizens can engage with complex, divisive issues and reach thoughtful, broadly supported conclusions. These are not isolated curiosities. They are consistent evidence that sortition-based deliberation works, and that it works precisely because it removes the adversarial incentive structure that elections impose.

Sortition also eliminates gerrymandering, one of the most powerful tools of partisan entrenchment. If legislators are not elected from geographic districts, there are no districts to manipulate. The entire grotesque industry of partisan map-drawing—which allows politicians to choose their voters rather than allowing voters to choose their politicians—becomes irrelevant.

V. Sortition Empowers Ordinary People

The democratic promise of elections is that they give every citizen an equal voice in selecting their leaders. This promise is, in practice, a fiction. The barriers to running for office—financial, social, professional, psychological—ensure that the candidate pool is drawn from a tiny and deeply unrepresentative slice of the population. The barriers to meaningful participation as a voter—the complexity of issues, the distortion of information by partisan media, the sheer difficulty of evaluating candidates' likely performance based on campaign rhetoric—ensure that voting often functions more as an expression of tribal identity than as an exercise in informed democratic choice.

Sortition delivers what elections only promise: genuine political equality. Under random selection, every eligible citizen has an equal probability of being chosen to serve. A nurse, a truck driver, a teacher, a small business owner, a stay-at-home parent, a construction worker—any of them could be called to participate in governance, just as any of them can currently be called to serve on a jury. This is not merely symbolic. It is a fundamental structural guarantee that the legislature will, with high statistical reliability, mirror the demographic composition of the citizenry. If 51 percent of the population is female, approximately 51 percent of the legislature will be female. If 13 percent of the population is Black, approximately 13 percent of the legislature will be Black. If 60 percent of the population lacks a college degree, approximately 60 percent of the legislature will lack a college degree. No electoral system in history has achieved this kind of descriptive representation, and no electoral system can, because elections inherently select for a narrow set of traits (ambition, charisma, fundraising ability, media savvy) that are not evenly distributed across demographic groups.

The epistemic argument for sortition is as powerful as the representational one. Hélène Landemore and other democratic theorists have drawn on insights from cognitive science and collective intelligence research to argue that groups composed of cognitively diverse members—diverse in life experience, professional background, knowledge base, and problem-solving approach—consistently outperform groups of individually expert but cognitively homogeneous members. This is the "diversity trumps ability" theorem formalized by Scott Page and Lu Hong, and it has profound implications for institutional design. A Congress composed of randomly selected citizens would possess an enormously broader range of life experience and practical knowledge than a Congress composed of lawyers and career politicians. The nurse would bring knowledge of healthcare delivery that no policy paper can replicate. The truck driver would bring understanding of supply chains and labor conditions. The small business owner would bring insight into regulatory burden. The veteran would bring firsthand knowledge of military life. This is not a sentimental argument about the wisdom of "regular folks." It is a rigorous claim, supported by mathematical models and empirical evidence, that cognitive diversity enhances collective decision-making quality.

The objection that ordinary citizens lack the competence to govern is both empirically unfounded and philosophically dangerous. It is empirically unfounded because the evidence from citizens' assemblies consistently demonstrates that randomly selected citizens, given adequate time, information, and facilitation, produce high-quality policy recommendations—often of higher quality than those produced by elected legislators, who are subject to donor pressure, partisan distortion, and reelection anxiety. It is philosophically dangerous because it leads inexorably to authoritarianism. If the argument is that ordinary people are too ignorant or too irrational to govern, then the logical conclusion is not elections—which suffer from the same alleged irrationality of the same public—but some form of epistocracy or technocratic rule by experts. Those who defend elections while attacking sortition on competence grounds are caught in a contradiction: they trust ordinary people to choose their rulers but not to be their rulers. The jury system exposes this contradiction daily. We trust randomly selected citizens, with no specialized legal training, to decide questions of guilt and innocence, life and death, in criminal trials. If citizens are competent to render those judgments, the claim that they are incompetent to deliberate on legislation is difficult to sustain.

Sortition transforms the citizen's relationship to government from passive to active, from spectator to participant. Under the current system, the average citizen's political role is reduced to voting every two or four years—a brief, largely symbolic act that rarely feels consequential. Under sortition, every citizen lives with the genuine possibility that they may be called to serve, that governance is not someone else's job but potentially their own. This shift in civic consciousness could have profound downstream effects on political engagement, civic education, and social solidarity. A society in which anyone might govern is a society in which everyone has a reason to be informed, engaged, and responsible.

VI. Answering the Objections

No proposal this transformative can escape serious objections. The most common deserve direct and honest engagement.

"Randomly selected citizens won't have the expertise to govern." This objection rests on a misunderstanding of what legislators actually do—and what they should do. Legislators are not, and should not be, subject-matter experts in every policy area. Their role is to weigh competing values, listen to expert testimony, represent the interests and perspectives of the public, and make judgment calls about tradeoffs. These are precisely the tasks that citizens' assemblies have shown randomly selected people can perform well, when given proper institutional support. The key is not selecting for pre-existing expertise but designing institutions that provide adequate information, facilitation, and deliberation time. Moreover, the current system does not select for expertise either. It selects for campaign skill. There is no reason to believe that the ability to win a fundraising race correlates with the ability to craft sound climate, healthcare, or immigration policy.

"People won't want to serve." Some will not, and a well-designed system should accommodate refusals while providing powerful incentives for participation: generous compensation, job protection, childcare, housing support during service, and the honor and civic gravity of the role. The jury system already requires compulsory service from citizens, and while jury duty is not universally beloved, it functions. Legislative service under sortition would be far better compensated and more meaningful. The deeper point is that a certain amount of reluctance is actually healthy. The philosophers have long noted that those who most eagerly seek power are often those least suited to wield it. A system that draws in people who did not seek office may be less susceptible to the pathologies of ambition than one that rewards only those who crave power.

"This would be unconstitutional." It would indeed require constitutional amendments, which is precisely what makes it a serious structural proposal rather than a legislative half-measure. The difficulty of amendment is not an argument against its desirability. The abolition of slavery required a constitutional amendment. Women's suffrage required a constitutional amendment. The direct election of senators required a constitutional amendment. If sortition is the right system, the constitutional barriers are reasons for sustained advocacy, not reasons for abandoning the idea.

"Bad actors could manipulate the random selection process." This is a legitimate concern that demands rigorous institutional safeguards—transparent randomization algorithms, independent oversight bodies, public auditing of the selection process, and severe penalties for tampering. These are solvable engineering and governance problems, and they are far simpler to solve than the currently unsolvable problem of money in electoral politics. We already trust randomization processes in contexts with enormous stakes: jury selection, the military draft lottery, scientific clinical trials. Extending that trust to legislative selection, with appropriate safeguards, is eminently feasible.

"This eliminates voter choice and democratic agency." This objection assumes that voting for candidates is the essence of democracy. That assumption is historically provincial. For most of the history of democracy—in its Athenian origins—sortition was considered the democratic method and elections the oligarchic one. Democracy means rule by the people, not rule by elected representatives of the people. Sortition provides a more literal and more reliable form of popular rule: the people themselves, in a statistically representative sample, are the government. The democratic agency shifts from the passive act of choosing a representative to the active possibility of being chosen to govern. This is, arguably, a richer and more meaningful form of democratic participation.

VII. Toward a Sortition Republic

The transition need not be abrupt. The United States could begin by establishing sortition-based citizens' assemblies at the local and state level to deliberate on specific policy questions, as France, Ireland, and other nations have done. It could create a randomly selected advisory chamber alongside the existing Congress, allowing the public to observe the quality of its deliberations. Over time, as the demonstrated competence and legitimacy of sortition bodies build public confidence, the case for replacing electoral institutions with sortition-based ones would become increasingly compelling.

What is needed first is a shift in imagination—a willingness to question the assumption, so deeply ingrained that it feels like natural law, that elections are synonymous with democracy. They are not. Elections are one method of organizing collective self-governance, and they are a method that has been thoroughly captured by wealth, distorted by partisanship, and hollowed of genuine popular power. Sortition is another method—older, in many ways simpler, and in crucial respects more democratic.

Conclusion

The American republic faces a confluence of crises—spiraling inequality, institutional paralysis, civic disintegration, collapsing public trust—that share a common root in the failure of electoral politics to deliver on the promise of democratic self-governance. The diagnosis is not that Americans chose the wrong candidates. The diagnosis is that the mechanism of competitive elections systematically empowers the wrong incentives: the incentive to raise money rather than solve problems, to demonize opponents rather than seek common ground, to serve donors rather than constituents, to seek reelection rather than the public good.

Sortition strikes at every one of these pathologies simultaneously. It eliminates the money, because there are no campaigns to fund. It eliminates the partisanship, because there are no parties to enforce discipline. It eliminates the careerism, because there are no careers to protect. It eliminates the oligarchic capture, because wealth cannot purchase what only chance bestows. And it replaces the narrow, unrepresentative political class that currently governs with a body that looks like, thinks like, and lives like the American people themselves.

Aristotle was right: the lot is democratic; election is oligarchic. It is time—long past time—for the world's most powerful republic to take its own democratic ideals seriously enough to consider the possibility that a better instrument exists. The lottery awaits. The question is only whether we possess the courage to trust ourselves.

  • A body of several hundred randomly chosen adults would, by probability, roughly reflect the actual demographics of a society—income levels, occupations, education, race, gender, age, disability status, geographic distribution
  • Current legislatures overwhelmingly consist of lawyers, businesspeople, and career politicians, creating a professional political class disconnected from ordinary experience
  • Proponents argue this means a sortition body would intuitively understand the effects of policies on working people, caregivers, renters, rural communities, and others chronically underrepresented
  • This isn't merely symbolic—research on citizens' assemblies suggests that participants from varied backgrounds introduce perspectives and practical knowledge that professional politicians simply lack

The deeper principle: Rather than choosing someone to speak for you, sortition means people like you are actually present in the room where decisions happen.

Argument 2: Reducing Elite Capture and Corruption

The core claim: Elections structurally favor concentrated wealth and organized power in ways that sortition would largely neutralize.

  • Campaign financing creates a dependency relationship between elected officials and donors. Sortition eliminates campaigns entirely, removing this lever of influence
  • Lobbying is effective partly because politicians need ongoing relationships with powerful actors for reelection. Randomly selected members serving single terms have no such incentive
  • Revolving door dynamics—where officials move between government and lucrative private sector positions—would diminish when officeholders are ordinary citizens returning to ordinary lives
  • Media manipulation and propaganda are designed to influence voter choice. Without elections to influence, the return on investment for such manipulation drops dramatically
  • Proponents like Guerrero argue that the current system creates what he calls "lottocracy's" opposite: a system where the same narrow interests repeatedly purchase influence regardless of which party wins

A structural point: The problem isn't necessarily that individual politicians are corrupt—it's that elections as a selection mechanism systematically filter for people responsive to concentrated power.

Argument 3: Eliminating Perverse Incentives of Electoral Politics

The core claim: The need to win elections distorts governance in predictable, damaging ways.

  • Short-termism: Politicians orient toward the next election cycle rather than long-term policy. Climate change, infrastructure investment, pension reform, and debt management all suffer from this
  • Partisan tribalism: Electoral competition incentivizes defining opponents as enemies rather than fellow citizens with different perspectives. Sortition members have no party label to defend
  • Performative politics: Elected officials spend enormous time on messaging, fundraising, and media appearances rather than deliberation. Studies suggest U.S. Congress members spend 30-70% of their time fundraising
  • Strategic voting and manipulation: Gerrymandering, voter suppression, and electoral system gaming become irrelevant
  • Risk aversion: Politicians avoid necessary but unpopular decisions. Randomly selected members serving a single term face no electoral punishment for making difficult choices supported by evidence

Argument 4: Improved Deliberation Quality

The core claim: Citizens freed from electoral pressures actually deliberate more thoughtfully than professional politicians.

This is supported by substantial empirical evidence from citizens' assemblies worldwide:

  • Ireland's Citizens' Assembly (2016-2018) tackled abortion, climate change, and aging populations, producing nuanced recommendations that broke through decades of political gridlock
  • British Columbia's Citizens' Assembly on Electoral Reform (2004) produced a sophisticated proportional representation proposal after months of study
  • France's Citizens' Convention on Climate (2019-2020) generated 149 detailed proposals after extensive expert consultation
  • Belgium's Ostbelgien model created a permanent citizens' council with real legislative input

Research findings from these experiments consistently show:

  • Participants take the responsibility seriously and engage deeply with complex material
  • They seek out and listen to expert testimony
  • They change their minds when presented with evidence
  • They find common ground across ideological lines more readily than elected politicians
  • They produce recommendations that are often more substantively detailed and internally coherent than typical legislation

Why this happens: Without the need to posture for cameras or appease donors, deliberation becomes genuine rather than theatrical.

Argument 5: Legitimacy and Trust

The core claim: Sortition could restore democratic legitimacy in an era of collapsing trust in institutions.

  • Public trust in legislatures across democracies has fallen to historic lows. Many citizens feel the system is "rigged" regardless of who they vote for
  • Sortition offers a fundamentally different social contract: anyone could be called to serve, and the body genuinely looks like the people
  • The principle is already accepted in the jury system—most people recognize that randomly selected citizens can make serious, high-stakes decisions (including life and death in criminal cases)
  • Proponents argue that knowing ordinary people made a decision—rather than a class of professional politicians—would increase public acceptance even of difficult policies
  • It addresses the growing sense that democracy has become an oligarchy with democratic aesthetics

Argument 6: Addressing Systemic Exclusion

The core claim: Elections contain built-in barriers that sortition bypasses.

  • Running for office requires money, connections, name recognition, free time, media skills, and often social privilege
  • This means self-selection bias ensures candidates are already disproportionately wealthy, educated, male, and from dominant social groups—before voters even make a choice
  • Voter participation itself is skewed by socioeconomic status, creating a feedback loop
  • Sortition with mandatory or strongly incentivized service would ensure representation of people who would never run for office: shift workers, single parents, people with disabilities, those without political connections
  • Some proposals include stratified random sampling to guarantee demographic proportionality

Proposed Implementation Models

Proponents aren't monolithic. Various models exist:

Full replacement models:

  • Randomly selected unicameral legislature with rotating membership
  • All legislative power transferred to sortition bodies

Hybrid models (more common among serious proposals):

  • One chamber elected, one chamber selected by lottery (analogous to how the House of Lords was historically non-elected)
  • Sortition bodies handle specific policy domains (Guerrero's "lottocratic" model)
  • Citizens' assemblies set agendas or review legislation, while elected bodies handle implementation
  • Sortition bodies draft constitutional amendments or handle issues where elected officials have conflicts of interest (redistricting, political ethics, electoral rules)

Common design features proposed:

  • Terms of 1-3 years with staggered rotation
  • Adequate compensation and job protection (like jury duty, but extended)
  • Access to independent expert staff and research
  • Structured deliberation processes
  • Transparency requirements
  • Training and orientation periods

Addressing Objections (As Proponents Frame Them)

Proponents have responses to the most common criticisms:

"Random people lack expertise"

  • Elected officials also lack expertise in most policy areas—they rely on staff, lobbyists, and committee briefings. Sortition members could access the same resources, minus the lobbyist influence
  • The diversity of life experience in a sortition body constitutes a form of distributed expertise that professional politicians lack

"People won't take it seriously"

  • Empirical evidence from citizens' assemblies consistently contradicts this
  • Most people, given genuine responsibility and adequate support, rise to the occasion—as the jury system demonstrates daily

"There's no accountability"

  • Proponents argue electoral accountability is largely a myth anyway—incumbency rates are extremely high, and voters have limited information
  • Sortition creates a different form of accountability: members are the public, so they bear the consequences of their own decisions when they return to private life
  • Some models include recall mechanisms or judicial review

"You might get extremists or incompetent people"

  • Statistical sampling makes it virtually impossible for extremists to constitute a majority
  • The deliberative structure moderates extreme positions—this is observed repeatedly in citizens' assemblies
  • Current systems already produce leaders many would characterize as extreme or incompetent, arguably more reliably than random chance would

Honest Caveats

Even a fair presentation should note:

  • Scale is untested. Citizens' assemblies have worked well at specific tasks, but no modern nation has implemented sortition as its primary governing mechanism. Extrapolating from small experiments to national governance involves genuine uncertainty
  • Implementation challenges are significant: ensuring genuine randomness, preventing manipulation of the selection process, managing transitions, handling foreign policy and crisis situations requiring continuity
  • The loss of electoral choice is a real tradeoff, not merely an illusion—some citizens genuinely value the ability to select specific leaders with specific visions
  • Powerful interests would resist the change intensely, raising serious questions about transition feasibility
  • There are tensions between sortition and other democratic values like political participation as self-governance (not just being governed by a statistical mirror)

Core Philosophical Summary

The deepest argument for sortition rests on a distinction between two conceptions of democracy:

  1. Democracy as choosing leaders — elections are the mechanism, and the quality of democracy depends on the quality of electoral competition
  2. Democracy as self-governance by the people — the question is whether the governing body genuinely is the people, and whether decisions reflect the informed judgment of ordinary citizens rather than the interests of a political class

Sortition advocates argue that we've conflated democracy so thoroughly with elections that we've forgotten elections were originally understood as the aristocratic selection method—designed to choose "the best" (aristos)—while lottery was the democratic one. They suggest that recovering this distinction might be essential to making democracy actually function as self-governance rather than as a legitimizing ritual for elite rule.

The growing body of real-world evidence from citizens' assemblies gives these arguments empirical grounding that purely theoretical proposals lacked a generation ago.

Political scientist Dr. Harold Fenwick of Georgetown University echoed the concern: "There's a real danger that randomly selected citizens might be too representative of the population.
