The Lottery of Liberty: A Speech for Sortition

Friends, fellow citizens, Americans —

I stand before you today to ask one dangerous question — a question our founders should have asked, a question that Athens asked twenty-five hundred years ago:

What if the cure for our broken republic... is trust in each other?

We have been taught — since childhood, since our first mock election in elementary school — that voting for representatives is the highest expression of democracy. That elections are democracy.

I'm here to tell you: they are not. They never were. And deep down... you already know it.

I. The Promise That Was Broken

We were promised a government of the people, by the people, for the people. Look around. What do we have?

A government of the wealthy, by the connected, for the donors.

Today, the average cost of winning a seat in the United States Senate exceeds $10 million. A House seat? Over a million. The presidency? Billions. Before a single vote is cast, before a single policy is debated, before a single citizen's voice is heard — a filter has already been applied. And that filter says: only the rich, only the ambitious, only the connected need apply.

Who runs for office in America? Not the nurse working double shifts in Tulsa. Not the electrician in Scranton. Not the teacher in Oakland. Not the farmer in Iowa. The people who actually understand the lives of ordinary Americans are structurally excluded from the system that claims to represent them.

Instead, we get dynasties. We get millionaires. We get career politicians who haven't held a private-sector job in thirty years. We get people who are exceptional — exceptionally ambitious, exceptionally wealthy, exceptionally willing to do whatever it takes to win.

And we wonder why they don't represent us.

Elections do not produce representation. Elections produce aristocracy. And that is not my opinion — that is the opinion of the very political philosophers who invented democratic theory. Aristotle said it plainly: "The appointment of magistrates by lot is thought to be democratic, and the election of them oligarchic."

He said that in 350 B.C., and we still haven't listened.

II. The Corruption Engine

Let's talk about what elections actually incentivize. Because a system is only as good as its incentives — and the incentives of electoral politics are rotten to the core.

To win an election, you need money. To get money, you need donors. To keep donors, you need to serve their interests. This is not a bug. It is the operating system.

Every single day in Washington, elected officials spend hours — not in committee, not reading legislation, not listening to constituents — but in call centers, dialing for dollars. They sit in cubicles across the street from the Capitol and they beg wealthy strangers for campaign contributions. Multiple members of Congress have admitted they spend thirty hours a week fundraising. Thirty hours! That is a full-time job — and it is not the job we hired them to do.

And what happens when the fundraising is done? Exposed to a tidal wave of lobbying. More than twelve thousand registered lobbyists descend on Capitol Hill — outnumbering members of Congress twenty to one. They write the bills. They shape the amendments. They host the dinners. And when a legislator leaves office? They become the lobbyist. The revolving door spins and spins, and every rotation greases it further.

Now — imagine, just imagine — a world where none of this exists.

Imagine legislators chosen by lottery. Random citizens, drawn from the population, called to serve — the way we call jurors today. No campaign. No donors. No war chest. No super PACs. No attack ads. No lobbyist breakfasts, because there would be no permanent political class to lobby.

You cannot corrupt a process that has no candidates. You cannot buy a seat that is allocated by chance. You cannot gerrymander a lottery. You cannot suppress a random draw.

Sortition doesn't just reduce corruption. It makes the machinery of corruption obsolete.

III. The Wisdom of Ordinary People

Now I hear the objection already — it's forming on your lips, it's buzzing in your mind. You're thinking: "But random people aren't qualified! We need experts! We need leaders!"

And I say to you, with the deepest respect: that is the voice of a system that taught you not to trust yourself.

Let me ask you this. Do you trust a jury? When a person's life is on the line — their freedom, their future — we entrust the decision to twelve randomly selected citizens. Not judges alone. Not lawyers. Not politicians. Ordinary people. And the institution of the jury is one of the most respected in our legal system. Why? Because ordinary people, given the facts and the time to deliberate, make remarkably good decisions.

This is not idealism. This is evidence.

Around the world, citizens' assemblies chosen by sortition have tackled some of the hardest issues of our time — and they have performed brilliantly:

  • In Ireland, a citizens' assembly of randomly selected people broke a decades-long political deadlock on abortion and marriage equality — issues that elected politicians were too afraid to touch. Their recommendations went to referendum and passed overwhelmingly.

  • In British Columbia and Ontario, citizens' assemblies designed sophisticated electoral reform proposals that experts praised for their quality and nuance.

  • In France, the Citizens' Convention on Climate produced 149 policy proposals after months of deliberation, consultation with experts, and genuine debate.

  • Deliberative polling experiments conducted by Professor James Fishkin at Stanford have shown, again and again, that when randomly selected citizens are given balanced information and time to discuss, their views become more nuanced, more informed, and more public-spirited.

These aren't flukes. They reveal a deep truth about human beings: we rise to the occasion when we are trusted with responsibility.

Elected politicians posture. They perform. They calculate every word for its effect on the next election. Randomly selected citizens have no such incentive. They have no election to win, no base to appease, no donor to satisfy. They can simply think. They can simply listen. They can simply ask: what is best for the country?

When was the last time you believed a politician was sincerely asking that question?

IV. True Representation

Here is perhaps the most powerful argument of all, and it is mathematical in its elegance:

A randomly selected legislature would, by the laws of probability, actually look like America.

Roughly half would be women. The racial composition would mirror our census. There would be people who earn minimum wage sitting beside small business owners. There would be veterans, students, retirees, immigrants, people with disabilities — the full, vibrant tapestry of this nation, woven into the fabric of governance.

Today, Congress is approximately 50% millionaires. In the general population, that figure is about 8%. Congress is overwhelmingly composed of lawyers and businesspeople. The average age skews older. The diversity that exists is hard-won and still insufficient.

This matters — not symbolically, but substantively. Research consistently shows that legislators' personal backgrounds influence their priorities. Wealthy legislators prioritize tax policy that benefits the wealthy. Legislators who have never experienced poverty design inadequate safety nets. Representatives who have never been denied healthcare don't feel the urgency of reform.

A sortition body wouldn't need to "represent" the people. It would BE the people.

The factory worker wouldn't need a lobbyist to make her case. She would be in the room. The veteran wouldn't need an advocacy group to explain what the VA system feels like from the inside. He would be at the table. The single mother, the immigrant shop owner, the young person drowning in student debt — they wouldn't be petitioning power. They would be exercising it.

This is not a radical idea. It is the original idea. It is the idea that burned in Athens for nearly two hundred years. The Athenians had a word for people who withdrew from public affairs and refused civic participation — idiotes. They understood something we have forgotten: that democracy is not a spectator sport, and citizenship is not merely the act of choosing which elite will rule over you.

V. The Design

Now — let me be clear. I am not proposing chaos. I am not suggesting we pull names from a hat tomorrow morning and hand over the nuclear codes by noon.

Sortition, like any system of government, requires thoughtful design. And scholars, political scientists, and democratic reformers have spent decades developing serious, detailed proposals. Let me sketch one possibility:

A Legislative Assembly of, say, 500 citizens chosen by stratified random lottery — ensuring demographic representativeness. Members would serve a single term of two to three years — long enough to develop expertise, short enough to prevent entrenchment. They would be compensated generously — at the level of current congressional salaries — so that no one is excluded by economic hardship.

They would be supported by non-partisan expert staffs — just as congressional committees currently rely on policy analysts and researchers. Members would participate in structured deliberation, hearing testimony from all sides, engaging with experts, and debating among themselves before voting.

For executive functions, we could employ a council model — a randomly selected executive council rather than a single president, reducing the concentration of power and the cult of personality that poisons our current system.

Term limits would be absolute. You serve once. You return to your community. There is no career to protect, no reelection to chase, no dynasty to build. You are a citizen who served, and you go home. Just as jurors do. Just as the Athenians did.

And here's what's beautiful: every single American would know that they might be called. Imagine what that does to civic culture. Imagine a nation where every adult knows that they might be the one making decisions next year. Would you pay more attention to policy? Would you engage more deeply with your community? Would you take governance more seriously?

Of course you would. Because it would no longer be their government. It would be yours.

VI. Answering the Fear

I know there is fear. Change of this magnitude should provoke serious questions. Let me address several honestly:

"What about demagogues and extremists?" Look around! Elections have not protected us from demagogues. In fact, elections reward demagoguery. The more extreme the rhetoric, the more attention it generates, the more donations it attracts. A lottery, by contrast, draws from the moderate center of the population. Statistical sampling gives you the mainstream, not the fringe.

"What about expertise?" Most current legislators are not policy experts. They are experts in getting elected — an entirely different skill. Under sortition, citizen-legislators would have access to the same expert testimony, the same research staff, the same analytical resources. The difference is they would have no political reason to ignore the evidence.

"What about accountability?" This is the most serious objection, and it deserves a serious answer. In our current system, the theory is that elections provide accountability — vote the bums out. But in practice? Incumbents win over 90% of the time. Gerrymandering creates safe seats. Name recognition and war chests make challengers nearly irrelevant. The "accountability" of elections is largely a myth. Under sortition, accountability comes from transparency, from public deliberation, from the knowledge that you must return to the community you've governed and look your neighbors in the eye.

"Hasn't this been tried?" Yes! For nearly two centuries in Athens — the most celebrated democracy in human history. In the republics of Venice and Florence. In the selection of juries across the common law world for hundreds of years. And in dozens of modern citizens' assemblies that have outperformed elected bodies on issue after issue.

VII. The Moral Case

But let me close not with mechanics, but with morality.

What is democracy? Strip away the rituals, the bunting, the "I Voted" stickers — what is it, really?

It is the radical assertion that no person is born to rule over another. That political authority belongs to all of us equally. That the janitor's voice is worth as much as the CEO's. That wisdom is distributed widely, not concentrated among the privileged few.

Elections betray this principle. They create a political class. They reward wealth, charisma, and ruthlessness. They filter out the humble, the honest, and the ordinary. They tell the vast majority of Americans: your role is to watch, to choose between options others have curated, and to hope for the best.

Sortition fulfills the democratic promise. It says to every citizen: you are worthy. You are capable. You might be called. And if you are, your nation trusts you.

Think about what it would mean for a young woman in Appalachia to know that she has the same chance of shaping national policy as any billionaire's son. Think about what it would mean for a Black man in Mississippi, whose grandparents were denied the vote, to sit in a legislative chamber not because he clawed his way through a brutal campaign, but because his country said: you belong here. Your perspective matters. Your judgment counts.

Think about what it would mean for trust. Right now, fewer than 20% of Americans trust Congress. Twenty percent! We have built a system that four out of five citizens regard with contempt. How long can a republic survive on that foundation?

Sortition offers something elections never can: legitimacy born from equality. Not the equality of the ballot box, where your vote is one in a hundred million and your choices are pre-selected — but the equality of genuine participation, where you yourself might govern.

VIII. The Call

My friends, I am not naive. I know that those in power will resist this. Of course they will. You do not ask an aristocracy to abolish itself. You do not ask the beneficiaries of a corrupt system to dismantle it voluntarily.

But I am not speaking to those in power. I am speaking to you.

You, who have watched election after election and felt that something was deeply wrong. You, who have voted for the "lesser evil" so many times you've forgotten what it feels like to vote for something. You, who have watched billionaires purchase influence while your letters to your representatives disappear into the void. You, who have felt, in your bones, that this government does not belong to you.

You are right. It doesn't. Not yet.

But it could.

We stand at a crossroads that every republic eventually reaches — the moment when the machinery of self-governance has been so thoroughly captured by wealth and faction that reform within the system becomes nearly impossible. The founders feared this moment. They debated it. Some of them — those we celebrate least — even proposed sortition as a safeguard.

We have the scholarship. We have the evidence. We have the models. We have the historical precedent. We have the moral clarity.

What we need now is the courage.

The courage to say that elections, as we practice them, have failed the democratic experiment. The courage to imagine something better. The courage to believe — truly believe — that ordinary Americans, chosen by lot, deliberating in good faith, supported by expertise and bound by transparency, can govern themselves better than any political class ever has or ever will.

The Athenians believed it. And they built a civilization we still study with awe.

I believe it. I believe it because I have seen what citizens' assemblies accomplish. I believe it because I have seen what juries accomplish. And I believe it because I know this nation — its people, its resilience, its stubborn, beautiful insistence that every person matters.

So let us begin this conversation. Let us demand pilot programs at the local level — sortition councils in our cities, our counties, our states. Let us build the evidence. Let us show the skeptics. And let us, step by step, reclaim the democracy we were promised.

Not government by the powerful. Not government by the privileged. Not government by the politicians.

Government by the people. Truly. Finally. At last.

Thank you.

"The best argument against elections is a five-minute conversation with a career politician. The best argument for sortition is a five-minute conversation with your neighbor."

In the cradle of modern democracy, the United States prides itself on a system of elections that promises representation for all. Sortition is not a utopian fantasy but a time-tested mechanism for fair representation. In this system, legislative bodies like Congress and executive leaders such as governors or even the president would be drawn randomly from eligible citizens, much like jury duty. Terms would be limited—perhaps two to four years—to prevent entrenchment, and participants would receive stipends, training, and expert advisors to ensure effective decision-making. Eligibility would be universal for adults, with basic safeguards like random audits to prevent fraud. This approach sidesteps the electoral circus, where candidates must amass fortunes and pander to special interests, and instead reflects the demographic diversity of the nation. According to the Center for Responsive Politics, the 2020 federal election cycle alone cost over $14 billion, with much of it flowing from corporate PACs and wealthy donors who expect favors in return. Politicians spend up to 70% of their time fundraising, as revealed by former lawmakers, leaving little room for genuine public service. This creates a quid pro quo culture: policies favoring Wall Street bailouts, fossil fuel subsidies, and tax breaks for the ultra-rich, while essential services like healthcare and education languish. Elected officials become beholden to donors, not voters, leading to scandals like the insider trading rampant in Congress, where members outperform the stock market by 17% annually.

Sortition flips this dynamic entirely. Random selection levels the playing field—no one buys their way in, because no one campaigns at all. Every citizen, from the factory worker in Ohio to the teacher in Texas, has an equal shot at serving, immune to the sway of lobbyists. Countries like Belgium have used sortition for advisory councils on contentious issues like euthanasia, yielding agreements that elected bodies couldn't achieve. By design, sortition incentivizes bridge-building, not trench warfare, healing the divides that elections exacerbate.

Finally, and most powerfully, sortition would empower ordinary people, fulfilling democracy's egalitarian ideal. Elections are an oligarchy in disguise: incumbents win 90% of races, and newcomers must be wealthy (self-funded or donor-backed) or famous. The average congressional candidate spends millions, pricing out all but the elite—over 50% of U.S. lawmakers are millionaires, compared to 3% of the population. In conclusion, the United States stands at a crossroads: cling to a flawed electoral machine that breeds corruption, division, and elitism, or embrace sortition to reclaim genuine self-rule. By removing the gates of money and party, sortition would purify politics, unite a fractured nation, and hand power back to the people who built it. A citizen selected by lot has no party platform to obey, no primary base to appease, no partisan whip threatening to end their career. They are free to consider evidence, change their mind, and vote their conscience.

Complex issues would be handled as they are now: through committees, hearings, expert testimony, and deliberation. Elections were a revolutionary technology for the 18th century. They were a vast improvement over hereditary monarchy. A nationwide system of sortition means filling legislative and executive offices by random lottery from the citizenry, rather than by election. It was used in ancient Athens, and in Venice, Florence, and other republics.

Proponents argue for it on these grounds:

1. Government Fairness - Equal Opportunity to Serve

The core argument for fairness is mathematical equality.

  • Equal chance: In a pure lottery, every eligible citizen has the exact same probability of being selected. In an election, that probability is heavily skewed by factors like charisma, wealth, education, and name recognition.
  • No incumbency advantage: Elections have a strong incumbency bias - over 90% of incumbents in the US House win re-election. Sortition eliminates career politicians entirely. Terms would be single and non-renewable.
  • Eliminates vote-counting disputes and gerrymandering: There are no districts to draw, no voter suppression, no strategic voting, and no disputes over vote totals. Selection is by verifiable random process.

2. Reducing Elite Influence

Proponents argue elections structurally filter for elites, while sortition structurally filters them out.

  • No campaign finance: There is no campaign to fund. That removes the need to raise money from donors, Super PACs, corporations, unions, and lobbyists. Proponents argue this breaks the donor-candidate dependency.
  • No party gatekeeping: You don't need party endorsement, media access, or connections to get on the ballot. Parties would have no mechanism to select, fund, or punish members.
  • No professional political class: Qualities that make someone electable - ambition for power, comfort with fundraising, media-trained speaking - are not the same as qualities that make someone a good representative. A lottery draws from people who would never run.
  • Harder to corrupt prospectively: You cannot bribe or invest in a candidate before they are selected because you don't know who will be selected. Lobbying would have to target 300+ random citizens after the fact, rather than a few predictable committee chairs you helped elect.

3. Enhancing Democratic Representation

The model used by most modern advocates is not pure random draw, but stratified sortition - a lottery weighted to create a body that is statistically representative of the population.

  • Descriptive representation: An elected Congress is disproportionately male, wealthy, college-educated, and from law/business backgrounds. A stratified random sample of 500 people would be roughly 50% women, would mirror the country's racial makeup, income distribution, geographic distribution, and mix of occupations - farmers, nurses, retail workers, engineers, etc.
  • Representation of interests without election incentives: Elected officials, proponents argue, must constantly think about re-election, primary challenges, and appealing to their base. A sortition-based legislator with one term and no re-election possibility has no electoral incentive to perform for a base, grandstand for cameras, or avoid compromise.
  • Reduction of polarization and partisan voting: Because members are not elected on a party platform and do not owe their seat to a party, there is no whip system and no partisan loyalty. Deliberation is supposed to be issue-by-issue rather than team-vs-team.
  • Cognitive diversity: Research on group decision-making shows that cognitively diverse groups often produce better solutions than groups of high-performing experts. A random sample maximizes that diversity.

In practice, most proposals envision it working like jury duty on a national scale: random selection from all eligible adults, with ability to opt out for hardship, a civic salary equivalent to a high professional wage, a term of 1-3 years, and support staff, expert briefings, and deliberative procedures to make informed decisions.
